title: Weak equivalences of Kan fibrations over arbitrary simplicial bases
statement: Use simplicial sets, weak homotopy equivalences and Kan fibrations of [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper]. Let $B$ be any small simplicial set, let $p:E\to B$ and $q:T\to B$ be Kan fibrations, and let $u:E\to T$ satisfy $qu=p$. For each vertex $b\in B_0$, define the strict simplicial fibers $E_b=E\times_B\Delta^0$ and $T_b=T\times_B\Delta^0$ using the constant simplex at $b$. These fibers are Kan complexes. Then $u$ is a weak homotopy equivalence if and only if every $u_b:E_b\to T_b$ is a weak homotopy equivalence. Neither $B$, $E$ nor $T$ is required to be a Kan complex; empty bases and empty fibers are allowed.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.7.1 (Kerodon Tag 00ZN), specializing the base weak equivalence to the identity. Its proof uses Ex-infinity to remove the Kan-base hypothesis. Read online, not archived in literature/. This is a Kerodon identifier, not a Stacks tag.

proof.text: First the strict fibers are Kan: a horn into $E_b$ is a horn into $E$ lying over the constant simplex at $b$; lift that constant simplex through $p$. Its filler still lies in $E_b$. A horn into $T_b$ gives a horn into $T$ over the constant simplex at $b$; the Kan lifting property of $q$ gives a simplex of $T$ over that constant simplex, hence a filler in $T_b$. Empty fibers have no horn maps, since every horn in positive dimension has a vertex. By [lem-coef-kan-realization-serre], $P=|p|:|E|\to|B|$ and $Q=|q|:|T|\to|B|$ are Serre fibrations, without a Kan hypothesis on any of these simplicial sets. By the natural finite-limit assertion of [lem-coef-realization-finite-limits], the fibers of $P,Q$ at the realized vertex $b$ are $F=|E_b|$ and $G=|T_b|$, and the induced map is exactly $f=|u_b|$. Put $U=|u|$; the square $(U,1_{|B|})$ strictly commutes. Apply [lem-coef-serre-homotopy-exact-sequence] to this square, at any chosen fiber vertex $e$ and its image $u(e)$. Write $i:F\to|E|$, $j:G\to|T|$ for inclusions and $\partial_E,\partial_T$ for connecting maps. All subsequent sequences, actions and path lifting are supplied by that node, and their comparisons have identity base maps. An empty fiber needs no pointed sequence. If a total-space component mapped to the base component of $b$, a path from the image of one of its points to $b$ would lift, producing a point in that fiber. Thus over a component with empty fiber there is no total-space component. In particular the component-orbit formula also holds in this case, with both sets empty.

proof.text: Assume $u$ is a weak homotopy equivalence, in the realization sense of [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper], and fix $b$. The natural orbit identifications of [lem-coef-serre-homotopy-exact-sequence] identify the map $\pi_1(|B|,b)\backslash\pi_0(F)\to\pi_1(|B|,b)\backslash\pi_0(G)$ with the map on total-space components over $[b]$. This is bijective, since $\pi_0(U)$ is bijective and $U$ is over the identity. The map $\pi_0(f)$ is equivariant for the same group $H=\pi_1(|B|,b)$. For each source orbit choose a vertex $e$ in a component of $F$; this is possible because every point of a realization is joined inside its representing simplex to a vertex. Its stabilizer is $\operatorname{im}(P_*:\pi_1(|E|,e)\to H)$, and the image stabilizer is $\operatorname{im}(Q_*:\pi_1(|T|,u(e))\to H)$. They are equal: $Q_*U_*=P_*$ and $U_*$ is an isomorphism. The map on these two transitive orbits is consequently bijective, since $h[e]$ and $h'[e]$ have the same image precisely when $h'^{-1}h$ belongs to their common stabilizer. Bijectivity on orbit sets then shows $\pi_0(f)$ itself is bijective. If $F$ is empty, its orbit set is empty, so the target orbit set and hence $G$ are empty too.

source.place: Proposition 3.2.8.1, component-action argument and exact-sequence diagram; agent expansion through realization and Serre fibrations to remove the Kan-base hypothesis, giving the fixed-base case of Proposition 3.3.7.1 (00ZN). Sources read online 2026-10-17; archival copies WANTED.

proof.text: Continue to assume $u$ is a weak equivalence. Fix a fiber vertex $e$ and $n\geq1$. Use the natural exact sequences of [lem-coef-serre-homotopy-exact-sequence]. If $a\in\pi_n(F,e)$ satisfies $f_*a=1$, then $U_*i_*a=j_*f_*a=1$; injectivity of $U_*$ gives $i_*a=1$. Write $a=\partial_E c$ with $c\in\pi_{n+1}(|B|,b)$. Naturality gives $\partial_T c=1$, so $c=Q_*d'$ for some $d'\in\pi_{n+1}(|T|,u(e))$. Lift $d'$ to $d$ through the isomorphism $U_*$. Then $P_*d=Q_*U_*d=c$, whence $a=\partial_EP_*d=1$. For surjectivity let $a'\in\pi_n(G,u(e))$ and lift $j_*a'$ through $U_*$ to $z\in\pi_n(|E|,e)$. Since $P_*z=Q_*j_*a'=1$, write $z=i_*a$. The element $a'(f_*a)^{-1}$ lies in $\ker j_*$, hence equals $\partial_Tc$ for some $c\in\pi_{n+1}(|B|,b)$. Naturality yields $f_*((\partial_Ec)a)=a'$. Thus $f_*$ is an isomorphism at every fiber vertex. The products are ordered as written, so the fundamental group case uses no commutativity.

proof.text: Conversely assume every $u_b$ is a weak homotopy equivalence. For each vertex $b$, $\pi_0(f)$ is a bijection equivariant for $\pi_1(|B|,b)$ by [lem-coef-serre-homotopy-exact-sequence]. Its inverse is equivariant too: apply equivariance and the inverse bijection to $h f(x)=f(hx)$. It therefore induces a bijection on orbit sets, including empty ones. The same node identifies these orbit sets with the total-space components mapping to $[b]$. Every component of $|B|$ contains a vertex, since a point is joined to a vertex inside its representing simplex. Choose one such vertex for each component; the resulting bijections over these components prove that $\pi_0(U)$ is bijective.

source.place: Proposition 3.2.8.1, component-action argument and exact-sequence diagram; agent expansion through realization and Serre fibrations to remove the Kan-base hypothesis, giving the fixed-base case of Proposition 3.3.7.1 (00ZN). Sources read online 2026-10-17; archival copies WANTED.

proof.text: Still assume all fiber maps are weak equivalences. Fix a vertex $e$ of $E$, put $b=p(e)$, and let $n\geq1$. In the natural exact sequences of [lem-coef-serre-homotopy-exact-sequence], suppose $a\in\pi_n(|E|,e)$ satisfies $U_*a=1$. Then $P_*a=Q_*U_*a=1$, so $a=i_*c$ for some $c\in\pi_n(F,e)$. Since $j_*f_*c=1$, exactness gives $f_*c=\partial_Td$ with $d\in\pi_{n+1}(|B|,b)$. By naturality and injectivity of $f_*$, $c=\partial_Ed$. Hence $a=1$. For surjectivity take $a'\in\pi_n(|T|,u(e))$ and put $d=Q_*a'\in\pi_n(|B|,b)$. Naturality sends $\partial_Ed$ to $\partial_Td$, the distinguished point. When $n=1$ the relevant fiber map is the bijection on $\pi_0$; when $n\geq2$ it is the isomorphism on $\pi_{n-1}$. Thus $\partial_Ed$ is the distinguished point. Exactness supplies $a\in\pi_n(|E|,e)$ with $P_*a=d$. Now $a'(U_*a)^{-1}=j_*c'$ for some $c'\in\pi_n(G,u(e))$. Lift $c'$ through $f_*$ to $c$. Then $U_*((i_*c)a)=a'$. Thus $U_*$ is an isomorphism at every total-space vertex in every positive degree, including the nonabelian degree one.

source.place: Proposition 3.2.8.1, component-action argument and exact-sequence diagram; agent expansion through realization and Serre fibrations to remove the Kan-base hypothesis, giving the fixed-base case of Proposition 3.3.7.1 (00ZN). Sources read online 2026-10-17; archival copies WANTED.

proof.text: For completeness, the vertex-based checks in steps 3 and 5 give the checks at every point required by the weak-equivalence definition of [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper]. A point of $|E|$ or $|E_b|$ is represented by a point of a standard simplex. The straight segment to one of its vertices realizes to a path to a vertex. Base-point transport along this path is an isomorphism on based homotopy groups: represent a class by a based cube, shrink the cube into an interior cube, and map its boundary collar along the path. Reversing the path defines the inverse; a path followed by its reverse contracts relative to its endpoints, giving the inverse homotopies. This construction commutes with continuous maps, so it conjugates the given homotopy-group map to its vertex-based map (for $n=1$ this is the usual path conjugation). Step 2 and step 3 therefore prove the forward implication, and step 4 and step 5 prove the reverse implication. If $B$ has no vertices, it has no simplices: every simplex has a vertex obtained by a face operator. Maps to $B$ then force $E=T=\varnothing$, so $u$ is the identity on the empty simplicial set and the fiber condition is vacuous. For nonempty $B$, the orbit arguments already cover empty fibers and total spaces. No Kan condition on $B,E,T$ was used.
